added_lemmas.statement:
For every fixed adoption calendar \(C\) admitted by \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\) with \(q>0\), there exist strictly positive rational shares \(p_g\) summing to one, deterministic balanced-panel sequences with \(n_g/N=p_g\), and a law \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\) supported on \((0,\infty)^T\) such that
\[
\mathbb E_P[Y_{gt}(1)]=\mathbb E_P[Y_{gt}(0)]\quad((g,t)\in U),
\qquad
\mathbb E_P[Y_{gt}(0)]=a_gb_t\quad(g\in C,\ 1\le t\le T).
\]
On the balanced, equal-observation-weight, no-covariate, no-offset intersection with the Moreau--Kastler individual-imputation specification, both normalized PPML fits exist uniquely, \(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MK}}^{\mathrm{ind}}=\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{CM}}\) samplewise, and
\[
\operatorname{AVar}_P\!\left(\sqrt N\{\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MK}}^{\mathrm{ind}}-\theta_{\mathrm{PTT}}\}\right)-V^{\star}
=\Gamma>0.
\]
The restriction of \(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{eff}}\), which is regular on the larger cohort-mean experiment, is therefore a strictly lower-variance regular competitor on this intersection.  Consequently the published Moreau--Kastler individual-imputation estimator is not universally semiparametrically efficient when \(q>0\).  This one-way conclusion neither identifies \(V^{\star}\) as the efficiency bound in the unrestricted richer individual-level experiment nor transfers the \(q=0\) cohort-mean efficiency conclusion to that experiment.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix an adoption calendar \(C\) admitted by \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\) and suppose \(q>0\).  Put
\[
p_g=|C|^{-1}\quad(g\in C),
\qquad
n_{g,k}=k,
\qquad
N_k=k|C|,
\tag{1}
\]
for integers \(k\ge1\).  These shares are strictly positive and rational, sum to one, and satisfy \(n_{g,k}/N_k=p_g\) exactly.  Choose any positive normalized factor vectors \(a,b\) and any strictly positive treated-cell means.  They determine a strictly positive interior observed mean vector \(m\), with \(m_{gt}=a_gb_t\) on \(U\).

Because \(q>0\), choose a nonzero sufficiently small covariance coordinate \(x\) in the fixed-support family.  The realizable-quadratic-loss theorem gives a corresponding \(P_\rho\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\) with mean \(m\), unchanged cycle Gram matrix \(K_0\succ0\), and
\[
\Gamma
=B^{-2}x^{\prime}D_\mu^{-1}K_0^{-1}D_\mu^{-1}x
>0.
\tag{2}
\]
The strict inequality follows because \(B>0\), every diagonal entry of \(D_\mu\) is positive, \(K_0^{-1}\succ0\), and \(x\ne0\).  This law is in fact supported on strictly positive outcomes.  Indeed, the bounded-family definition gives
\[
Y_{gt}=m_{gt}+s^0_{gt}\varepsilon_{gt},
\qquad
s^0_{gt}=\sqrt{\tau_0m_{gt}},
\qquad
0<\tau_0<\min_{g,t}m_{gt}.
\tag{3}
\]
Thus \(0<s^0_{gt}<m_{gt}\), and since \(\varepsilon_{gt}\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
Y_{gt}\ge m_{gt}-s^0_{gt}>0
\tag{4}
\]
at every support point.  The support is finite, so it is bounded and has finite fourth moments.

The causal completion in the same bounded-family definition sets \(Y_{gt}(1)=Y_{gt}(0)=Y_{gt}\) on \(U\), and sets \(Y_{gt}(0)=\mu_{gt}=a_gb_t\) on \(D\).  Consequently
\[
\mathbb E_{P_\rho}[Y_{gt}(1)]
=\mathbb E_{P_\rho}[Y_{gt}(0)]
\quad((g,t)\in U),
\qquad
\mathbb E_{P_\rho}[Y_{gt}(0)]=a_gb_t
\quad(g\in C,\ 1\le t\le T).
\tag{5}
\]
This proves average no anticipation and multiplicative parallel trends; consistency is part of the same completion.  In the Moreau--Kastler individual-effects notation the subclass is embedded by the cohort-constant choices \(\alpha_{gi}=\log a_g\) and time effects \(\beta_t^{\mathrm{MK}}=\log b_t\), with \(\beta_1^{\mathrm{MK}}=0\), equal observation weights, and no covariates or offsets.

For completeness, both sample PPML fits are finite and unique under this law.  Every realized untreated outcome is positive by (4).  Under the normalization of the first-period time effect, the individual untreated design has full column rank: if a perturbation obeys \(\delta\alpha_{gi}+\delta\lambda_t=0\) on every untreated observation, the period-one observations give \(\delta\alpha_{gi}=0\) for all \(g,i\), and the never-treated cohort's observations then give \(\delta\lambda_t=0\) for every \(t\).  The same argument, with one intercept per cohort, gives full column rank of \(X\).  For either design matrix \(W\), positive weights \(w_j\), and positive responses \(y_j\), the criterion
\[
\ell(\xi)=\sum_jw_j\{y_jW_j^{\prime}\xi-
\exp(W_j^{\prime}\xi)\}
\tag{6}
\]
has Hessian
\[
\nabla^2\ell(\xi)
=-W^{\prime}\operatorname{diag}
\{w_j\exp(W_j^{\prime}\xi)\}W\prec0.
\tag{7}
\]
It is also coercive.  Along any unbounded parameter sequence, pass to a subsequence whose normalized direction converges.  Full column rank supplies a nonzero limiting fitted-index direction.  If any fitted index diverges positively, its negative exponential term sends (6) to \(-\infty\); otherwise a fitted index diverges negatively, and its strictly positive response makes the corresponding linear term tend to \(-\infty\).  Hence every upper level set is bounded, so continuity and (7) give a finite unique normalized maximizer.  The aggregation-bridge proposition now applies to (1) and yields the exact sample identity
\[
\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MK}}^{\mathrm{ind}}
=\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{CM}}.
\tag{8}
\]

It remains to compare variances without importing an efficiency bound into a different experiment.  The cohort-mean PPML linearization gives asymptotic variance \(h_{\mathrm{CM}}^{\prime}\Omega h_{\mathrm{CM}}\).  The weighted-cycle and canonical-gradient results give
\[
J^{\prime}h_{\mathrm{CM}}=J^{\prime}h^{\star}=c,
\qquad
\ker(J^{\prime})=\operatorname{col}(R),
\qquad
R^{\prime}\Omega h^{\star}=0.
\tag{9}
\]
Therefore \(h_{\mathrm{CM}}-h^{\star}=R\gamma\) for some \(\gamma\), and multiplication by \(R^{\prime}\Omega\) gives
\[
b_{\mathrm{cyc}}=K\gamma,
\qquad
\gamma=K^{-1}b_{\mathrm{cyc}}.
\tag{10}
\]
Using (9)--(10), the definition of \(\Gamma\), and
\(V^{\star}=h^{\star\prime}\Omega h^{\star}\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_{\mathrm{CM}}^{\prime}\Omega h_{\mathrm{CM}}-V^{\star}
&=2h^{\star\prime}\Omega R\gamma
+\gamma^{\prime}R^{\prime}\Omega R\gamma\\
&=\gamma^{\prime}K\gamma
=b_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{\prime}K^{-1}b_{\mathrm{cyc}}
=\Gamma.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
Equations (2), (8), and (11) imply
\[
\operatorname{AVar}_{P_\rho}\!\left(
\sqrt{N_k}\{\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{MK}}^{\mathrm{ind}}
-\theta_{\mathrm{PTT}}\}\right)-V^{\star}
=\Gamma>0.
\tag{12}
\]

Finally, the efficient-attainment theorem says that \(\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is regular on the larger cohort-mean experiment and has variance \(V^{\star}\).  Restricting a regular estimator to the displayed Moreau--Kastler intersection preserves regularity, so (12) exhibits a regular competitor with strictly smaller variance.  This refutes universal efficiency of the individual-imputation estimator for every calendar with \(q>0\).  The argument uses \(V^{\star}\) as the attained variance of that competitor and as the cohort-mean bound only; it neither identifies the bound for the unrestricted richer individual-level experiment nor makes any assertion about individual-level efficiency when \(q=0\), where (2) supplies no strict-loss direction.
added_lemmas.justification: This mandated boundary corollary converts the exact aggregation bridge and the realizable positive cycle loss into a counterexample for the published individual-imputation procedure without exporting an efficiency bound across experiments.
added_lemmas.gap: Moreau--Kastler (2025, printed pp. 15 and 20--23, equations (3.1), (3.2), (3.13), (3.14), and (3.19)) defines the individual fixed-effects specification and imputation ratio but does not give a positive-cycle semiparametric nonuniversality result.
added_lemmas.consumer: Users of the Nagengast--Yotov regional-trade-agreement and Menkhoff--Miethe treaty and bank-deposit applications obtain a rigorous warning that exact aggregation does not make the published PPML estimator universally efficient.

prose_updates.tldr: At fixed \(T\), with a never-treated cohort, positive multiplicative untreated means, independent cohorts, arbitrary within-unit dependence, and finite fourth moments, one weighted tangent restriction arises from each untreated graph cycle. Bounded score truncation followed by an exact mean correction proves tangent completeness in the explicitly mean-differentiable experiment. The canonical gradient removes the covariance projection of the cohort-mean PPML influence onto the \(q\) cycle directions; a feasible correction attains the bound and supports pointwise Wald inference. The cohort-mean PPML estimator is efficient for every bounded legal covariance law exactly when \(q=0\); for \(q>0\), exactly \(q\) primitive balances characterize its exceptional efficient laws, and a bounded strictly positive fixed-support family has exact loss \(\Gamma>0\). On the balanced equal-weight, no-covariate, no-offset intersection with Moreau--Kastler, the individual and cohort-mean point estimators coincide, so the same family and the regular cycle-corrected competitor prove that the published individual estimator is not universally efficient when \(q>0\). This transfer is one-way: it gives neither the richer individual-level efficiency bound nor a \(q=0\) efficiency conclusion there. The regularized frontier for growing \(T\) and \(q\) remains open at \(\mathrm{oeq{:}growing\text{-}cycle\text{-}frontier}\).

project_justification.gap: Moreau--Kastler (2025, printed pp. 15 and 20--23, equations (3.1), (3.2), (3.13), (3.14), and (3.19)) gives an individual fixed-effects PPML specification, imputation ratio, and inference procedure; it does not characterize universal semiparametric efficiency by untreated-cycle topology. Wooldridge (2023) studies a richer individual-level nonlinear imputation framework, while existing efficient staggered-DiD results are additive and rank-one completion results do not classify covariance-sensitive efficiency for proportional treatment on the treated.
project_justification.niche: In the fixed-\(T\) cohort-mean experiment, positive rank-one means make graph cycles both the complete tangent restrictions and the available covariance-sensitive precision directions. The exact aggregation boundary then embeds a balanced equal-weight, no-covariate, no-offset subclass of the published Moreau--Kastler specification, allowing a strict \(q>0\) nonuniversality conclusion without claiming that the cohort-mean bound governs the unrestricted individual-level experiment.
project_justification.fill: The project proves weighted-cycle tangent completeness using bounded score truncation plus exact mean correction, derives the canonical gradient and the cohort-mean PPML influence, constructs an attaining covariance-weighted cycle correction, characterizes the efficient covariance laws by \(q\) independent primitive balances, and certifies exact positive quadratic loss on an open realizable bounded-law family. The aggregation bridge and positive-cycle corollary show that the published individual estimator inherits strict inefficiency on their precise intersection. The growing-\(T\), growing-\(q\) regularized frontier remains open at \(\mathrm{oeq{:}growing\text{-}cycle\text{-}frontier}\).

prose_updates.related_work: Moreau--Kastler (2025, printed pp. 15 and 20--23, equations (3.1), (3.2), (3.13), (3.14), and (3.19); \url{https://taxobservatory.world/www-site/uploads/2025/05/WP31_-Proportional-Treatment-Effects-in-Staggered-Settings.pdf}) specifies individual fixed effects and time effects, imputes individual untreated counterfactuals, aggregates a treated observed-to-predicted ratio, and develops inference. The aggregation proposition proves point-estimator coincidence with the cohort-mean rank-one PPML procedure only for balanced panels with equal observation weights, no covariates or offsets, and exact equality between target and sample cohort shares. Point-estimator coincidence alone does not transfer efficiency bounds. The positive-cycle corollary instead uses the regular cohort-mean cycle correction as a strictly better competitor on that intersection, which is sufficient to refute universal efficiency for \(q>0\), but it does not assert that \(V^{\star}\) is the unrestricted individual-level bound or that \(q=0\) yields individual-level efficiency. Wooldridge (2023, Sections 2--3) studies fully interacted individual-level nonlinear imputation and does not supply the cohort-mean cycle frontier. Ciani and Fisher (2019, printed page 7, Section 3.1 and Appendix B) note and simulate possible PPML inefficiency; the present fixed-horizon result supplies necessity, sufficiency, exact codimension, and a realizable strict-loss neighborhood. Kir\'aly, Theran, and Tomioka (2015, Theorem 34 and Remark 35) identify even cycles as rank-one matrix circuits. Chamberlain (1987) and Newey (1990) provide general efficiency and score tools, while the support-preserving bounded-score truncation and exact mean correction are proved here for this nonnegative panel. Roth and Sant'Anna (2023), Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess (2024), and Chen, Sant'Anna, and Xie (2025) concern covariance-aware additive staggered designs rather than this proportional ratio. Nagengast--Yotov and Menkhoff--Miethe are motivating applications; their richer dependence and fixed effects remain outside the benchmark. No theorem here resolves the growing-\(T\), growing-\(q\) regularized problem posed at \(\mathrm{oeq{:}growing\text{-}cycle\text{-}frontier}\).
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: Because \(\infty\in C\) and the panel is fully observed, \(q=\sum_{g<\infty}(g-2)\); the topology theorem does not claim arbitrary missing-panel graph generality. There is no positive loss bound uniform over all inefficient laws because \(\Gamma(x)\to0\) as \(x\to0\). Singular covariance blocks, zero mean cells, random cohort shares, growing \(T\), unbalanced panels, and dyadic shared-country dependence are outside the formal model. The finite-fourth-moment tangent result is pointwise for the explicitly mean-differentiable differentiable-in-quadratic-mean experiment and uses bounded support-preserving submodels constructed by truncation and exact mean correction; it does not classify tail-escaping paths for which score-moment differentiation fails. The Moreau--Kastler transfer is confined to the balanced equal-weight, no-covariate, no-offset intersection with exact shares: strict \(q>0\) loss transfers because a regular lower-variance competitor restricts to that intersection, but neither the cohort-mean bound nor the \(q=0\) efficiency conclusion transfers to the unrestricted richer individual-level experiment.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The fixed-horizon contributions are PTT-specific weighted-cycle completeness, constructive tangent equality for the explicitly mean-differentiable finite-fourth-moment experiment, the exact rank-\(q\) primitive covariance map, the acyclic universal-efficiency equivalence for the cohort-mean estimator, and a bounded strictly positive family with exact quadratic loss and an ambient positive-radius strict-loss neighborhood. The feasible covariance-weighted correction attains the cohort-mean bound and supports pointwise inference. Exact equality with Moreau--Kastler's individual estimator is confined to balanced equal-weight panels without covariates or offsets and with target shares equal to sample shares. On that intersection, the \(q>0\) family yields a strictly better regular competitor and therefore refutes universal efficiency of the published individual estimator; no unrestricted individual-level bound and no \(q=0\) individual-level efficiency result is claimed. Canonical projection algebra and routine sandwich consistency are supporting machinery. The growing-horizon, growing-cycle-rank regularized frontier remains open at \(\mathrm{oeq{:}growing\text{-}cycle\text{-}frontier}\).

statement_notes.justification: The proposition proves a deterministic point-estimator identity under exact aggregation conditions; that identity is needed for the positive-cycle counterexample but, by itself, transfers no semiparametric efficiency bound.
statement_notes.gap: Moreau--Kastler (2025, printed pp. 15 and 20--23, equations (3.1), (3.2), (3.13), (3.14), and (3.19)) presents the individual specification and imputation estimator but not the profiling identity with the cohort-mean rank-one score or any cross-experiment efficiency transfer.
statement_notes.consumer: Applied users can test whether their implementation lies on the exact aggregation boundary and can avoid treating point-estimator coincidence as evidence that two statistical experiments share an efficiency bound.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix the interior mean vector \(m\) and suppose \(q>0\).  Let
\[
\mathcal E=U\setminus\mathcal T_0
=\{(g,t):g<\infty,\ 2\le t<g\}
\]
index the \(q\) fundamental cycles.  The definition of \(\tau_0\) gives, for every observed coordinate,
\[
0<s^0_{gt}=\sqrt{\tau_0m_{gt}}<m_{gt}.                 \tag{1}
\]
For a finite cohort \(g\), the mass function in the definition of \(P_\rho\) obeys
\[
2^{-T}\left[1+\sum_{t=2}^{g-1}\rho_{gt}e_te_g\right]
\ge
2^{-T}\left[1-\sum_{t=2}^{g-1}|\rho_{gt}|\right]>0.   \tag{2}
\]
Its masses sum to one because each nonconstant Rademacher character has zero sum on \(\{-1,1\}^T\).  Orthogonality of those characters also yields
\[
\mathbb E_\rho[\varepsilon_{gj}]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E_\rho[\varepsilon_{gj}^2]=1,
\qquad
\mathbb E_\rho[\varepsilon_{gt}\varepsilon_{gg}]=\rho_{gt}
\quad(2\le t<g),                                      \tag{3}
\]
and every other distinct-coordinate covariance is zero.  Consequently the observed vector
\(Y_g=m_g+s_g^0\odot\varepsilon_g\) has mean \(m_g\), marginal variances \((s^0_{gj})^2\), and its only off-diagonal covariances are
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_{P_\rho}(Y_{gt},Y_{gg})
=s^0_{gt}s^0_{gg}\rho_{gt}=x_{gt},
\qquad (g,t)\in\mathcal E.                             \tag{4}
\]
Every vertex of the hypercube has positive probability by (2).  If \(v\ne0\), the function \(e\mapsto v^{\prime}(s_g^0\odot e)\) is not constant on that hypercube, because changing a coordinate with \(v_js^0_{gj}\ne0\) changes its value.  Hence
\(v^{\prime}\Sigma_g(\rho)v>0\), so each covariance block is positive definite.  Equation (1) gives
\[
0<m_{gj}-s^0_{gj}\le Y_{gj}\le m_{gj}+s^0_{gj}<\infty. \tag{5}
\]
There are finitely many cohorts and coordinates, so (5) supplies a common finite bound and all fourth moments are finite.

Take independent draws from this vector law within each cohort and independent samples across distinct cohorts, retaining the fixed positive shares and sample-size sequences from \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\).  Use the potential-outcome completion specified in the definition of \(P_\rho\): observed and untreated potential outcomes agree on \(U\), the observed and treated potential outcomes agree on \(D\), and the missing untreated outcome on \(D\) is the constant \(\mu_{gt}\).  Consistency and no anticipation then hold, and
\(\mathbb E_PY_{gt}(0)=\mu_{gt}=a_gb_t\) at every cohort--time cell.  Positivity follows from the positive-factor assumption.  Together with the stipulated stratified sampling and shares in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\), (2)--(5) prove
\[
P_\rho\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathbb E_{P_\rho}Y=m.                                \tag{6}
\]

We next calculate the loss without an approximation.  At \(\rho=0\),
\[
\Sigma_{g0}=\operatorname{diag}((s^0_{g1})^2,\ldots,(s^0_{gT})^2)
=\tau_0\operatorname{diag}(m_g).
\]
Because \(m_{gt}=\mu_{gt}\) on \(U\), the untreated coordinates of the product of the base covariance and the PPML coefficient are
\[
(\Omega(0)h_{\mathrm{CM}})_U
=\tau_0M P_U^{-1}h_{\mathrm{CM},U}
=\tau_0MX S^{-1}c_\beta.                              \tag{7}
\]
The weighted-cycle theorem gives \(R^{\prime}J=0\); since \(R_D=0\) and \(J_U=MX\), it follows from (7) that
\[
b_{\mathrm{cyc}}(0)=R^{\prime}\Omega(0)h_{\mathrm{CM}}=0. \tag{8}
\]
Every perturbation in (4) connects the untreated coordinate \((g,t)\) to the treated coordinate \((g,g)\).  It therefore leaves the untreated--untreated covariance block unchanged.  Since every column of \(R\) is supported on \(U\),
\[
K(x)=R^{\prime}\Omega(x)R
=R^{\prime}\Omega(0)R=K_0.                            \tag{9}
\]

For completeness, calculate the response of every cycle coordinate directly.  From the definitions of \(\Omega\), \(\alpha^{\mathrm{CM}}\), and \(F\), for every \((g,j)\in U\),
\[
(\Omega h_{\mathrm{CM}})_{gj}
=\frac1{p_g}\sum_{s=1}^T
\operatorname{Cov}_P(Y_{gj},Y_{gs})h_{\mathrm{CM},gs}
=\mu_{gj}F_{gj}.                                      \tag{10}
\]
Thus the row associated with the fundamental cycle \(e=(g,t)\) satisfies
\[
r_e^{\prime}\Omega h_{\mathrm{CM}}
=F_{g1}-F_{gt}-F_{\infty1}+F_{\infty t}.              \tag{11}
\]
On a treated cell, the PPML coefficient definition gives
\[
\alpha^{\mathrm{CM}}_{gg}
=h_{\mathrm{CM},gg}/p_g=1/B.                          \tag{12}
\]
The covariance change in (4) consequently changes \(F_{gt}\) by
\(x_{gt}/(B\mu_{gt})\).  It changes none of the other four terms in (11), and a perturbation indexed by a different element of \(\mathcal E\) changes none of the terms in this cycle response.  Combining (8), (11), and (12), in the ordering of the columns of \(R\), gives the exact diagonal map
\[
b_{\mathrm{cyc}}(x)
=-B^{-1}D_\mu^{-1}x.                                  \tag{13}
\]
The base covariance \(\Omega(0)\) is positive definite by positive shares and positive diagonal variances, while \(R\) has rank \(q\) by the weighted-cycle theorem.  Hence \(K_0\succ0\).  Substitution of (9) and (13) into the cycle-loss definition gives
\[
\Gamma(x)
=B^{-2}x^{\prime}D_\mu^{-1}K_0^{-1}D_\mu^{-1}x.       \tag{14}
\]
The matrix in (14) is positive definite because \(B>0\), \(D_\mu\) has a positive diagonal, and \(K_0\succ0\).  Therefore \(\Gamma(x)>0\) for every nonzero admissible \(x\).

It remains to prove ambient, rather than merely pathwise, realizability.  Suppose
\(\|\Sigma-\Sigma_0\|_{\mathcal A}<\delta_0\).  For each cohort, the Rayleigh quotient and the definition of \(\delta_0\) imply
\[
\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_g)
\ge \lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{g0})
-\|\Sigma_g-\Sigma_{g0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
>\lambda_0/2>0.                                        \tag{15}
\]
Let \(A_g=\Sigma_g^{1/2}\), \(A_{g0}=\Sigma_{g0}^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(s_g^0)\), and \(Q_g=A_g-A_{g0}\).  Direct multiplication shows that
\[
A_gQ_g+Q_gA_{g0}=\Sigma_g-\Sigma_{g0}.
\]
The integral
\[
Q_g=\int_0^\infty
e^{-uA_g}(\Sigma_g-\Sigma_{g0})e^{-uA_{g0}}\,du
\]
solves this Sylvester equation.  Taking operator norms and integrating the exponential bounds gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|Q_g\|_{\mathrm{op}}
&\le
\frac{\|\Sigma_g-\Sigma_{g0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}
{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_g)}+
 \sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{g0})}}\\
&<\frac{\delta_0}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}}.                 \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(\varepsilon_g\) now have independent Rademacher coordinates and set
\(Y_g=m_g+A_g\varepsilon_g\).  Then \(\mathbb E Y_g=m_g\) and
\(\operatorname{Var}(Y_g)=\Sigma_g\).  Since
\(\|\varepsilon_g\|_2=\sqrt T\), equations (1), (16), and the defining upper bound on \(\delta_0\) imply, coordinatewise,
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{gt}
&=m_{gt}+s^0_{gt}\varepsilon_{gt}+(Q_g\varepsilon_g)_t\\
&\ge m_{gt}-s^0_{gt}-\sqrt T\|Q_g\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
&>d_0-\frac{\sqrt T\delta_0}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}}
>d_0/2>0.                                               \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, (16) gives the uniform coordinatewise upper bound
\[
Y_{gt}
\le m_{gt}+s^0_{gt}+\frac{\sqrt T\delta_0}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}},
\]
so these laws share a finite outcome envelope over the whole covariance ball.  Take independent draws within cohorts and independent samples across cohorts.  Applying the same potential-outcome completion used in (6), and using (15), proves
\[
\mathbb B_{\mathcal A}(\Sigma_0,\delta_0)
\subset\mathcal L(m).                                  \tag{18}
\]

Equation (13) also proves that the linear map \(\mathcal L_m\) has rank \(q\): for each coordinate \(e=(g,t)\in\mathcal E\), a sufficiently small admissible choice \(x=ue_e\), with \(u\ne0\), maps to the nonzero multiple
\(-u(B\mu_{gt})^{-1}e_e\), and these \(q\) images span \(\mathbb R^q\).  In particular \(\|\mathcal L_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}>0\).  Because \(q>0\), choose one such coordinate and then choose \(|u|>0\) still smaller if necessary.  The defining strict inequality for \(\rho\) remains valid, and continuity of the finite-dimensional covariance path at \(u=0\) ensures
\(\|\Sigma(ue_e)-\Sigma_0\|_{\mathcal A}<\delta_0\).  Set \(x_0=ue_e\).  Then
\[
\|\Sigma(x_0)-\Sigma_0\|_{\mathcal A}<\delta_0,
\qquad
\mathcal L_m(\Sigma(x_0))
=-B^{-1}D_\mu^{-1}x_0\ne0.                            \tag{19}
\]
Both arguments in the minimum defining \(\eta_0\) are therefore positive.  If
\(\|\Sigma-\Sigma(x_0)\|_{\mathcal A}<\eta_0\), the triangle inequality and the first radius restriction give
\[
\|\Sigma-\Sigma_0\|_{\mathcal A}<\delta_0,            \tag{20}
\]
so (18) implies \(\Sigma\in\mathcal L(m)\).  Linearity and continuity of \(\mathcal L_m\), followed by the second radius restriction, give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathcal L_m(\Sigma)\|_2
&\ge \|\mathcal L_m(\Sigma(x_0))\|_2
-\|\mathcal L_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}
  \|\Sigma-\Sigma(x_0)\|_{\mathcal A}\\
&>\tfrac12\|\mathcal L_m(\Sigma(x_0))\|_2>0.         \tag{21}
\end{aligned}
\]
For every covariance in this ball, positive shares and covariance interior imply \(\Omega\succ0\); full column rank of \(R\) then implies \(K=R^{\prime}\Omega R\succ0\).  Equations (20)--(21) and the cycle-loss definition yield
\[
\mathbb B_{\mathcal A}(\Sigma(x_0),\eta_0)
\subset\mathcal L(m)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Gamma=b_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{\prime}K^{-1}b_{\mathrm{cyc}}>0
\]
throughout that ambient open ball, completing the proof.

Fix the interior mean \(m\) and the positive share vector \(p\), and write
\(\mathcal E=\{(g,t):g<\infty,\ 2\le t<g\}\) for the non-tree untreated edges.  First observe that the PPML coefficient is feasible for the target derivative.  The weighted-cycle theorem gives \(\dim\ker(J^{\prime})=q\).  Since \(J\) has \(|U|+|D|\) rows and \(|C|+T-1+|D|\) columns, the identity \(q=|U|-|C|-T+1\) implies that \(J\) has full column rank.  Its block structure then implies that \(X\) has full column rank.  Positive weights consequently make
\(S=X^{\prime}P_UMX\) positive definite.  Since \(M\) and \(P_U\) are commuting positive diagonal matrices, the definitions of \(J\), \(h_{\mathrm{CM}}\), and \(c\) give
\[
J^{\prime}h_{\mathrm{CM}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
X^{\prime}MP_UXS^{-1}c_\beta\\
(p_g/B)_{(g,t)\in D}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}c_\beta\\c_D\end{pmatrix}
=c.                                                     \tag{1}
\]
The covariance-interior and positive-share assumptions give \(\Omega\succ0\).  Direct substitution in the definition of \(h^\star\) gives
\(J^{\prime}h^\star=c\), and Lagrange minimization of
\(h^{\prime}\Omega h\) subject to \(J^{\prime}h=c\) gives this unique minimizer.

By the weighted-cycle theorem, every feasible difference is in
\(\ker(J^{\prime})=\operatorname{col}(R)\).  Therefore, when \(q>0\), write
\(h^\star-h_{\mathrm{CM}}=R\gamma\).  Moreover
\[
\Omega h^\star
=J(J^{\prime}\Omega^{-1}J)^{-1}c,
\]
so \(R^{\prime}\Omega h^\star=0\) because \(R^{\prime}J=0\).  It follows that
\[
0=R^{\prime}\Omega(h_{\mathrm{CM}}+R\gamma)
=b_{\mathrm{cyc}}+K\gamma.
\]
Since \(R\) has full column rank and \(\Omega\succ0\), \(K\succ0\), and hence
\[
h^\star=h_{\mathrm{CM}}-RK^{-1}b_{\mathrm{cyc}}.       \tag{2}
\]
The orthogonality just established and (2) give the Pythagorean identity
\[
h_{\mathrm{CM}}^{\prime}\Omega h_{\mathrm{CM}}
-h^{\star\prime}\Omega h^\star
=b_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{\prime}K^{-1}b_{\mathrm{cyc}}
=\Gamma.                                               \tag{3}
\]
For \(q=0\), the same identities hold with empty cycle matrices: the weighted-cycle theorem gives \(\ker(J^{\prime})=\{0\}\), so the two feasible coefficients in (1) coincide and \(\Gamma=0\).

The cohort-mean PPML linearization identifies
\(h_{\mathrm{CM}}^{\prime}Z\) as the estimator's influence function and its root-\(N\) asymptotic variance as
\(h_{\mathrm{CM}}^{\prime}\Omega h_{\mathrm{CM}}\).  The canonical-gradient theorem identifies \(h^{\star\prime}Z\) and \(V^\star=h^{\star\prime}\Omega h^\star\) as the canonical gradient and information bound.  Thus (3), or equivalently the primitive-balance characterization, proves at every fixed law that
\[
\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{CM}}\text{ is efficient}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
b_{\mathrm{cyc}}=0.                                   \tag{4}
\]

If \(q=0\), the right side of (4) is vacuous, and hence the estimator is efficient at every bounded law with the fixed \(m\) and \(p\).  Conversely, suppose \(q>0\).  The realizable-quadratic-loss theorem supplies, for this same \(m\), a nonzero admissible \(x\) and a law \(P_\rho\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{bd}}\) for which
\[
\Gamma(x)
=B^{-2}x^{\prime}D_\mu^{-1}K_0^{-1}D_\mu^{-1}x>0.     \tag{5}
\]
At that law, (3) and (5) show that the PPML asymptotic variance strictly exceeds the canonical bound.  It is therefore false that PPML is efficient at every fixed-mean bounded law.  This proves the asserted topological equivalence.

For an arbitrary realizable covariance at the fixed mean, the definition of \(\mathcal L_m\) and (4) give
\[
\{\Sigma\in\mathcal L(m):\widehat\theta_{\mathrm{CM}}
\text{ is efficient at }\Sigma\}
=\mathcal L(m)\cap\ker(\mathcal L_m).                 \tag{6}
\]
The exact diagonal response in the realizable-quadratic-loss theorem maps the \(q\) symmetric covariance directions
\(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{gt},Y_{gg})\), \((g,t)\in\mathcal E\), to
\(-e_{gt}/(B\mu_{gt})\).  These images are linearly independent because \(B\mu_{gt}>0\).  Since the codomain of \(\mathcal L_m\) is \(\mathbb R^q\),
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal L_m)=q.                  \tag{7}
\]
Thus its kernel is a proper codimension-\(q\) linear subspace when \(q>0\); the ambient realizability and strict-loss balls from the realizable-quadratic-loss theorem show that both the classification and its strict complement occur for legal bounded outcome laws, rather than only for formal covariance perturbations.

Finally, let \(0<\lambda_{\min}(K)\le\lambda_{\max}(K)\) be the extreme eigenvalues of \(K\).  Applying the Rayleigh quotient to \(K^{-1}\) gives
\[
\frac{\|b_{\mathrm{cyc}}\|_2^2}{\lambda_{\max}(K)}
\le
b_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{\prime}K^{-1}b_{\mathrm{cyc}}
\le
\frac{\|b_{\mathrm{cyc}}\|_2^2}{\lambda_{\min}(K)}. \tag{8}
\]
The middle term is \(\Gamma\) by definition.  Equations (4)--(8) provide necessity, sufficiency, exact codimension, and a sharp spectral characterization for the cohort-mean estimator.  The final comparison in the theorem is therefore a positioning statement: none of these mathematical conclusions is taken as a premise from Ciani and Fisher's observation or simulations.
